constraints: Cloud backups are end-to-end encrypted. logic.ts deriveCloudKey runs PBKDF2 on the password with salt `hrt-cloud-v1:${userId}` (600k iterations) to make an AES-GCM key, and the worker `content` table only ever holds ciphertext. No server-side feature (push, remote MCP, calendar feed) can read doses, labs, weight or templates unless the client uploads a separate plaintext projection.

The only health data the server can read today is the share snapshot in dosage_shares.snapshot_json: mode, timezone, events and a calibrated simulation sampled down to 2500 points. It deliberately leaves out lab values and body weight (shareSnapshot.ts). PUT /api/shares/live gives each link fresh random event ids. So a remote MCP built on this data has no labs and no weight, and cannot re-simulate projections server-side unless new opt-in fields are added.

sanitizeShareSnapshot in worker.ts rejects any extras key not in SHARE_EXTRA_KEYS ('extras contains an unsupported field'), and buildSharedDosageSnapshot copies extras wholesale. So a new ExtraKey (for example an injection site) makes PUT /api/shares/live return 400. useLiveShareSync then retries 4 times and gives up without telling anyone. New keys must be stripped client-side or allowlisted.

Live snapshots refresh only while the app is open. useLiveShareSync pushes 2 s after a change, and again on focus and every 5 minutes. The simulation grid ends at max(last dose + 14 d, now + 24 h) at upload time. Remote tools must return an as_of timestamp, and they cannot give a current estimate more than 14 days after the last dose.

The server cannot write into user records. Anything an assistant or a notification adds has to be an inbox item or proposal that the client merges. Local writes go through useAppData stamp() so updatedAt is set for syncMerge's newest-wins rule.

A new synced record kind must be wired in all of these places, or it silently fails to sync or gets dropped: syncMerge.ts RecordKind/RECORD_KINDS/CONTENT_FIELDS/emptyTombstones/normalizeSyncState, useAppData MODE_SUFFIXES (adoptSignedOutData), buildExportPayload, and a sanitizer. sanitizeImportedEvents rebuilds each event from id/route/timeH/doseMG/ester/extras/updatedAt only, so a new top-level DoseEvent field (note, site) is stripped on import and when a cloud sync is installed.
DoseEvent.extras is Partial<Record<ExtraKey, number>> and holds numbers only. Categorical data has to be an index, the way gelSite indexes GEL_SITE_ORDER.
Quick doses are per-device and never synced. doseTemplates are synced, so schedules should extend the template concept.

Each cloud backup is capped at 2 MiB (MAX_CLOUD_BACKUP_BYTES). The server keeps 5 revisions, and content writes are limited to 20 per minute. Journal text must be bounded, and photos cannot go into the backup.

D1 hit the 500 MB cap on 2026-09-21 (now on Workers Paid, 10 GB). D1 has a single primary, so writes are the scarce resource. Every new server table (push subscriptions, fire times, assistant links, activity log, inbox) must be capped per user and swept by cron, and must not write on every read.

The only cron is '17 */6 * * *' (housekeeping every 6 hours), which is far too coarse for reminders. Reminders need an extra cron every 1 to 5 minutes, with scheduled() branching on controller.cron. The self-hosted Docker image runs `wrangler dev`, which as far as I know does not fire cron triggers by itself. Server-sent reminders (and the existing sweep) would not run there without an external trigger, so in-app reminders and ICS must stay as fallbacks.

The PWA uses vite-plugin-pwa generateSW (registerType autoUpdate) and has no push or notificationclick handlers. Adding them needs injectManifest (keeping the /share navigateFallbackDenylist) or importScripts. A service worker cannot read localStorage, where all app data and auth_token live, so it needs an IndexedDB mirror of reminder labels and its own per-subscription secret.

Browsers have no reliable way to fire a scheduled local notification (the Notification Triggers API was abandoned). Reminders while the app is closed need Web Push with VAPID keys: the private key as a wrangler secret, the ES256 JWT via jose (already a dependency), and RFC 8291 payload encryption via WebCrypto in the worker. iOS supports Web Push only for PWAs installed to the home screen (16.4 and later), and Safari/iOS show no notification action buttons.

Push fire times stored on the server reveal when the person takes their doses. The worker already treats this as sensitive: it withholds updated_at on locked shares for exactly that reason. Reminder push must be opt-in, upload only opaque ids and a short horizon of timestamps, and send payloads with no medication name.

Bearer tokens never go in URLs. Share tokens live in the /share/#fragment and in POST bodies, and wrangler.toml observability has head_sampling_rate = 1, so every request is logged. A remote MCP connector must authenticate through an Authorization header with OAuth 2.1, not a token in the connector URL.

Session JWTs last 7 days, go idle after 3 days, and every non-admin token needs a sid row. The middleware also rejects any token that carries a `purpose` claim. A long-lived, revocable assistant credential therefore needs its own token type and table.

The Tauri shell is v1 (tauri ^1.8). The allowlist only has shell.open, invoke_handler is empty, csp is null, and @tauri-apps/api is not a dependency. Native notifications need the notification allowlist plus a cargo feature, and v1 cannot schedule a notification for later, so the app must keep running (system tray) for desktop reminders. A local MCP server needs new Rust code, since there is no IPC today.
Rate limiting uses fixed binding classes of 10, 20, 30, 60 and 300 requests per minute, and a missing binding fails open. New endpoints must use one of these classes or add a binding.

PDF export (src/services/export.ts) uses jsPDF forced to English 'to avoid font issues with non-Latin characters'. It is two raw tables with no chart. A localised clinician summary needs either embedded CJK fonts (several MB) or an HTML print route.
The Cloudflare worker CSP is default-src 'self', so any consent page or preview must be same-origin. CORS is Access-Control-Allow-Origin '*' on all API routes.

The simulation is an estimate. DoseAdvisory deliberately bases warnings on logged doses rather than the curve. Projections and what-if views must be labelled as estimates and must not act as dosing advice, and an assistant must never log anything without confirmation.

logic.ts simulation and calibration are pure TypeScript and portable, but the cloud crypto uses window.crypto. Reuse in Node, the worker or a sidecar needs globalThis.crypto. Calibration is expensive: for EKF/MIPD, buildClearanceField re-simulates 21 clearance knots, each up to 100k grid points. Projections that re-run calibration must be memoised, debounced, or moved to a Web Worker.
Every new string needs translations for the 7 UI languages (zh, zh-TW, yue, en, ja, ko, tr) in src/i18n/translations.ts, and layouts must hold up with CJK and long Turkish text.

features.name: Dose schedules and reminders (with calendar export and travel handling)
features.userValue: Missed or late doses are the most common real-world problem. People on weekly or 5-day injections and 3.5-day patch changes lose track easily. Logging with one tap from the reminder also keeps the curve accurate, because the model is only as good as the log.
features.ux: Setup: after 3 or more similar doses, Home shows a suggestion card: 'You have injected estradiol valerate 4 mg every 7 days lately. Remind you next Thursday at 20:00?' with [Set up reminder] and [Not now]. Settings > Reminders > New schedule: pick a saved dose template or the last dose. Then choose the cadence from plain presets for the route: injection 'Every 7 days / every 5 days / custom'; patch 'Twice a week, Monday and Thursday / weekly / follow each patch's wear time'; oral or sublingual 'Daily at 08:00 / twice daily at 08:00 and 20:00'; CPA 'Daily / every other day'. Choose the anchor ('Count from my last dose' or 'Same weekday every time'), the time, a lead ('On time / 15 min early / 1 h early') and 'Show medication name in notifications' (off by default). Delivery screen, with status written as words and icons: 'While the app is open' (always available); 'Even when the app is closed' (asks notification permission and sign-in, and says plainly that the server will know reminder times but not the medication); 'Desktop app'; 'Add to my calendar' (.ics download). Home: a 'Next up' line under the level readout reads 'Next injection Thursday 20:00, in 2 days'. When due, it becomes 'Estradiol valerate 4 mg is due now' with a primary [Log it] (pre-filled, editable) and secondary [Snooze 1 hour] and [Skip this one]. Notification: title 'Time for your dose', or the medication name if enabled, with 'Taken' and 'Snooze 1 h' action buttons on Chrome, Android and Windows. Tapping it opens a pre-filled 'Log this dose?' sheet with a time choice: 'Now, 20:07' or 'At the reminder time, 20:00'. Doses logged through the action button show 'Logged from a notification at 20:03' with Undo on the next open. History: the heatmap marks missed slots with an outline and names late ones in the tooltip, and a summary reads '12 of 13 doses on time in the last 90 days'. Travel: when the device time zone differs from the schedule's, a banner asks 'You are on Tokyo time now. Keep daily pills at 08:00 local time, or stay on Berlin time?' Injection intervals stay absolute. Extras: the installed app icon shows a badge while a dose is due, a long-press shortcut offers 'Log a dose', and the desktop tray shows the next dose.
features.technicalFit: Data: a new synced RecordKind 'schedules' that extends DoseTemplate (useAppData.ts and DoseForm.tsx: name/route/ester/doseMG/extras). It adds cadence {interval everyH | weekdays+time | daily times[] | patchWear}, anchor ('last_dose' | 'fixed'), tz (IANA, validated the way isValidIanaTimezone does), leadMin, showName, channels, pausedUntil and updatedAt. Wire it into syncMerge.ts (RECORD_KINDS, CONTENT_FIELDS, emptyTombstones, normalizeSyncState), useAppData (MODE_SUFFIXES, buildExportPayload, a new sanitizeImportedSchedules) and the stamp() writers. Scheduler: a new pure src/services/schedule.ts with nextOccurrences(schedule, events, nowH, horizonH). The floating anchor is the last event with the same route and ester plus everyH. Patches use the last patchApply.timeH + extras[ExtraKey.patchWearH] (that key already exists; PatchFields offers 3.5 and 7 day presets). inferSchedule(events) takes the median gap of at least 3 same-route, same-ester doses within ±10%. adherence() matches events to slots within a window and feeds DoseHeatmap. In-app delivery: a useReminders hook on the existing 60 s currentTime tick in useAppData calls registration.showNotification. Web Push: in vite.config.ts switch VitePWA to strategies 'injectManifest' with src/sw.ts (precache plus the /share denylist, then push and notificationclick handlers). The service worker reads labels from an IndexedDB mirror the app writes. Worker: migration 0006_push.sql with push_subscriptions(id, user_id, endpoint, p256dh, auth, secret_hash, created_at, last_ok_at) and push_fires(id, subscription_id, fire_at, rid), indexed on fire_at and capped at about 100 rows per subscription. Routes: POST /api/push/subscribe, PUT /api/push/fires (the client replaces its next 14 days), DELETE /api/push/subscribe/:id, and POST /api/push/ack and /api/push/snooze, which authenticate with the per-subscription secret held by the service worker, not the session JWT. Use RL_PER_MINUTE_30. VAPID_PUBLIC_KEY is a var and VAPID_PRIVATE_KEY a secret. The ES256 JWT is signed with jose, and the aes128gcm payload uses WebCrypto ECDH P-256 + HKDF. In wrangler.toml [triggers], add '*/5 * * * *' next to '17 */6 * * *'. scheduled() branches on controller.cron: the fast cron sends due fires, and the 6-hourly one prunes subscriptions that returned 404 or 410. 'Taken': the service worker writes {rid, takenAt} to an IndexedDB reminder-inbox, and the app drains it on start and on visibilitychange through addEvent. Cloud sync and live share then pick it up as normal. Tauri: add 'notification-all' and 'system-tray' to the tauri features in src-tauri/Cargo.toml, set allowlist.notification in tauri.conf.json, add @tauri-apps/api v1, and detect window.__TAURI__. v1 cannot schedule, so a JS timer runs while the tray keeps the process alive. ICS: generate the file client-side (file-saver is already a dependency) with RRULE FREQ=DAILY;INTERVAL=n or FREQ=WEEKLY;BYDAY=MO,TH (the 3.5-day patch becomes Mon/Thu) plus VALARM. Badge: navigator.setAppBadge. Shortcuts: add a manifest.shortcuts entry in vite.config.ts.
features.privacy: Schedules live only on the device and in the E2E backup, like templates. Web Push is opt-in. The server stores the push endpoint and keys plus a rolling 14-day list of fire timestamps, each with an opaque random id: not the schedule id, and no ester or dose. The payload carries only that id, and the service worker renders the text from the local mirror, discreet by default. The screen names the tradeoff (fire times reveal a dosing rhythm, the same concern behind withholding updated_at on locked shares) and offers local-only reminders and ICS instead. Calendar exports default to neutral titles, because calendars sync to Google or iCloud. Signing out removes the subscription and its fires, and account deletion cascades.

features.name: Plan ahead: projected curve and what-if regimen comparison
features.userValue: Shows where levels are heading if the schedule is kept (for example 'low point next Wednesday about 140 pg/mL'), what a late or missed dose does, and how a change the prescriber suggested would compare (4 mg every 7 days against 3 mg every 5 days) before trying it. It also shows when a new pattern settles, which is what lab timing depends on.
features.ux: Home chart: the past curve stays solid, and the next 4 weeks continue from the 'now' line as a dashed line, with planned doses as hollow tick marks and the caption 'Projected if you keep your schedule'. A 'Show plan' toggle sits in the chart's range bar. 'What if…' opens a sheet pre-filled with the current schedule, with editable dose, interval and route or ester. The alternative draws as a second dashed line in another tone, with plain-language comparison rows: 'Typical low point: about 150 pg/mL (now 120)', 'Typical high point: about 310 (now 260)', 'Time in 100 to 200 pg/mL: 64% vs 48%', 'Settles into the new pattern after about 3 weeks'. A fixed footer reads: 'Estimate from your model and labs, not a prescription. Talk to your clinician before changing your dose.' Actions: [Save as my schedule] (logs no dose) and [Add to visit summary]. When a dose is due, the card offers 'What if I take it tomorrow instead?' with a small preview.
features.technicalFit: runSimulation(events, bodyWeightKG) in logic.ts already stretches the grid to max(last event + 14 d, now + 24 h), so appending planned DoseEvents from nextOccurrences() extends the curve naturally. Run it as a separate useMemo (projectionSim) in useAppData, so planned events never enter `events` state, never sync, and never reach buildSharedDosageSnapshot or MCP. For calibration, calibration.factorFn is bound to the baseline sim's clearance field, so the projection has to call computeCalibration(projectionSim, events+planned, weight, labResults, method, historyMode). For EKF/MIPD that means 21 clearance-knot re-simulations (KMUL_STEPS), so debounce input by 250 ms, memoise per plan, and move to a Web Worker if slow. OU-Kalman's correction reverts on the OU_TAU_H = 336 h timescale. Metrics (low point, high point, time in range) come from interpolateConcentration_E2 × factorFn, or interpolateConcentration_T, over the last full cycle. Settling time is about 5 × the slowest effective half-life, the same rate logic as computeMaxLifetimeH. Target bands reuse the ranges in useAppData currentStatus (100 to 200 pg/mL; 300 to 1000 ng/dL). ResultChart.tsx gets optional `projection`, `alternative` and `plannedEvents` props, drawn dashed through the existing linePath, with a tooltip suffix 'projected'. Depends on schedules (feature 1), or falls back to 'repeat my last interval'.
features.privacy: Runs entirely on the device. Planned and what-if doses are temporary: they are left out of the backup, share snapshots and MCP unless the user saves one as a schedule. Nothing leaves the device unless the user exports it.

features.name: Lab planner tied to calibration
features.userValue: Labs are the model's only ground truth, but people often draw at random points in their cycle, which calibrates poorly. The planner says when to draw (the low point just before the next injection), when the model needs more labs, and when to recheck after a dose change, and it reminds them.
features.ux: Lab page, top card 'Your next blood test': 'Best time: Thursday morning, before your 20:00 injection (your low point). Ask the lab to note the draw time.' A reason line adapts to the state: 'Your model has 1 lab. Two more at different points in your cycle will let it learn how fast your body clears estradiol.', or 'Your model matches your labs within ±14%. Next check suggested around 12 Nov, 6 weeks after your dose change.' Buttons: [Remind me] (the day before and that morning) and [Add to calendar]. The Home chart shades the suggested draw window with a flat translucent band. After a lab is saved, a confirmation reads 'Saved 184 pg/mL. Your model now reads 12% higher for you.' with a small measured-vs-model comparison. A short checklist in plain words: 'Draw before your dose, not after', 'Use the same lab if you can', 'Write down the exact time'.
features.technicalFit: Built on CalibrationResult from computeCalibration (n, fitErrPct, kMul, halfLifeDeltaPct, points) and the logic.ts constants MIN_LABS_FOR_CLEARANCE = 3 (clearance only moves with 3 or more labs), OU_TAU_H = 336 (how fast OU information goes stale) and CAL_MEAS_SD. A new pure suggestLabDraw(events, schedules, calibration, nowH) works as follows. With an injection or patch schedule, the draw slot is the next planned dose minus 1 to 12 h. If every existing lab sits at a similar cycle phase, it suggests a different phase so clearance becomes identifiable. A regimen change detected in events (dose or interval) triggers a recheck after about 5 effective half-lives, or at least 4 weeks. The model counts as stale when the last lab is older than about 90 days, or older than 2 × OU_TAU_H in OU mode. The lab reminder is a schedule kind 'lab' in feature 1 and uses the same channels. UI: a card in src/pages/Lab.tsx, the explanation in CalibrationSettings.tsx, and a `highlightWindow` prop on ResultChart.tsx. The wording is a suggestion; the clinician decides how often to test.
features.privacy: Computed on the device. Lab reminders use the same opaque push path with generic text, and no lab values leave the device.

features.name: Supply and refill tracker
features.userValue: Running out of vials, patches or pills (pharmacy delays, weeks-long shipping, lapsed prescriptions) causes gaps that crash levels. 'About 23 days left, reorder by 2 Oct' prevents that. It also tracks when a vial was opened and how many needles are left, and can show how many millilitres to draw.
features.ux: Settings > Supplies (also a section on the History tab), one row per item: 'Estradiol valerate 40 mg/mL, 10 mL vial: about 6.2 mL left, lasts until 14 Nov on your schedule', 'Needles: 9 left', 'Patches 100 µg/day: 5 left, about 2.5 weeks'. Add-supply sheet: type (vial, pills, patches, gel, needles or syringes, other), medication picked from templates, strength (mg/mL, mg per tablet, µg/day per patch), quantity, opened on, optional 'use within' days, and 'It usually takes about 3 weeks to arrive'. Linking: 'Count down when I log estradiol valerate injections', plus a dead-space setting (default 0.05 mL per draw). Home warning, shown once the lead time is reached: 'Refill soon: your estradiol valerate runs out around 14 Nov. Reorder by 24 Oct to have it in time.' with [I've reordered] and [Remind me]. Dose form: under the dose it shows '4 mg is 0.10 mL of your 40 mg/mL vial'. When the tracked stock hits zero, it asks 'Your tracked vial is empty. Start a new one?'
features.technicalFit: A new synced RecordKind 'supplies' in syncMerge.ts (plus CONTENT_FIELDS, tombstones, sanitizer, buildExportPayload and MODE_SUFFIXES). Each item: {id, kind, route, ester, strength, unit, quantity, openedAtH, useWithinDays?, leadDays, deadSpaceML?, retiredAtH?, updatedAt}. Remaining stock is derived, never stored as a counter: quantity minus the consumption of matching events with openedAtH ≤ timeH < retiredAtH. Injections use doseMG / mg per mL + dead space, oral uses doseMG / mg per tablet, and each patchApply is 1. Deriving it keeps the tracker safe under syncMerge's union-by-id and newest-updatedAt-wins merge, where two devices decrementing a stored counter would lose one edit. The run-out date comes from schedule nextOccurrences (feature 1), or the median usage of the last 30 days as a fallback. Refill alerts are a reminder kind. ExtraKey.concentrationMGmL exists, but InjectionFields.tsx never collects it (only OnboardingCurve sets it), so the vial record becomes the source of concentration and gives DoseForm.tsx the mL-to-draw line.
features.privacy: Kept on the device and in the E2E backup. Never included in share snapshots, push payloads, or MCP unless that scope is turned on. Any source or vendor note is optional free text, stays local, and is never sent to the server, because where medication comes from can be sensitive.

features.name: Assistant integration (MCP)
features.userValue: Lets people ask an AI assistant in plain language from Claude Desktop, Claude Code or other MCP clients, without copying data by hand. Examples: 'What is my estimated E2 right now?', 'Did I miss any doses this month?', 'Summarise my last three labs for my endo', 'Log my shot, 4 mg EV just now'.
features.ux: Settings > Assistant, step 1 'Choose how your assistant connects'. Three cards with plain tradeoffs: 'On this computer' (desktop app; recommended; nothing is uploaded), 'Through your account' (a connector for web assistants; uploads a read-only copy of only what you choose, like a live share link), and 'Local helper' (for technical users; decrypts your backup on your own machine). Step 2 'What can it see?': toggles with counts. Dose history (on), estimated levels (on), schedules and adherence (on), lab results (off by default for the account option), supplies (off), journal (off, labelled 'includes your notes'). Time range: last 90 days, 1 year, or everything. Permission: 'Read only' or 'Read and suggest new entries, which you approve one by one'. Expiry: 7, 30 or 90 days, up to 1 year. Step 3 'Connect': copy-ready config for Claude Desktop and a `claude mcp add` command. For the account option, the server URL, then an in-app consent screen when the assistant connects: 'Claude wants to read your doses and estimated levels for 30 days' with [Allow] and [Deny]. Connected state: 'Connected to Claude, last used today at 14:02', a scope summary, 'Access ends 23 Oct' with [Extend], and a destructive [Revoke access] that asks for confirmation. Activity log: 'Today 14:02, read dose history (last 30 days, 9 entries)', 'Today 14:03, suggested a dose, approved by you'. A pending-suggestion card on Home: 'Your assistant suggested logging estradiol valerate 4 mg, injection, today 20:05' with [Add], [Edit] and [Discard]. Nothing is saved until approved. Standing notice: 'Whatever the assistant reads is sent to the company that runs it, for example Anthropic or OpenAI.' Tools: get_current_estimate (E2 or T plus CPA, unit, calibrated or not, fit ±%, as_of, band text, disclaimer); get_level_series(from, to, max_points ≤ 500); list_doses(from, to, limit ≤ 200), with readable names and ISO times with time zone; list_labs (measured, model at that time, ratio); get_calibration_summary (method, n, scale, half-life change, fit error, next suggested lab); get_schedule_and_adherence(days); get_supply_status; project_levels(plan), only on-device because it needs body weight; propose_dose and propose_lab, which return 'pending your confirmation'. Resource hrt://summary; prompt 'prepare_visit_summary'. Read tools are annotated readOnlyHint. There are no edit or delete tools.
features.technicalFit: (a) Desktop, recommended. src-tauri/src/main.rs has an empty invoke_handler and the allowlist only has shell.open. Add a command assistant_publish_state(json) that the web layer calls on a debounce, like useLiveShareSync's 2 s push. The payload comes from a new src/services/assistantSnapshot.ts that reuses buildSharedDosageSnapshot's sampling plus the scoped labs, calibration summary and schedules. Rust writes it to the app data directory with 0600 permissions. The same binary started with `--mcp` runs a stdio MCP server with no window (for example with the rmcp crate) and answers from that file, including as_of. Proposals go to an inbox directory that the running app watches through a Tauri event and turns into a confirm sheet. The activity log stays local. (b) Remote. Worker routes under /mcp using stateless Streamable HTTP JSON-RPC; no Durable Object is needed because the tools are request/response. Migration: assistant_links(id, user_id, token_hash, scopes, expires_at, snapshot_json, client_name, created_at, updated_at, last_used_at), capped at 5 per user; assistant_activity(link_id, at, tool, count), capped at 50 per link; assistant_inbox(id, user_id, sealed, created_at), capped at 20 per user. The cron sweeps them like sweepExpiredShares. Snapshot upload copies PUT /api/shares/live: the client pushes a projection, and the server runs it through a v2 of sanitizeShareSnapshot with optional labs and schedules, giving each link random event ids. Auth: OAuth 2.1 with PKCE and dynamic client registration, as in the MCP authorization spec; @cloudflare/workers-oauth-provider can handle this. The consent page is a new ViewKey behind the normal session. Access tokens are their own type in their own table, not session JWTs, which idle out after 3 days and are rejected when they carry a `purpose`. Rate limit with RL_PER_MINUTE_60 per link. The snapshot only refreshes while the app is open, so each result carries as_of; the estimate comes from the uploaded calibrated series, which runs to the last dose + 14 days. propose_* seals the item on arrival to a P-256 public key the app registered (ECDH + AES-GCM via WebCrypto), so D1 stores only ciphertext. The app drains the inbox on useCloudSync's triggers, asks the user, then calls addEvent or addLabResult and deletes the item. (c) Local helper. A Node package fetches /api/content and /api/content/:id and decrypts with the key from deriveCloudKey, on the user's machine. logic.ts needs globalThis.crypto instead of window.crypto for this. It runs runSimulation and computeCalibration locally. Writes are merged with syncMerge.mergeSyncStates and uploaded as a stamped, encrypted revision, which the app picks up through normal sync. This option needs a long-lived, scoped device token, not a stored password.
features.privacy: The desktop option keeps everything on the machine except what the assistant reads. The account option is explicitly the same as a live share: a plaintext copy on the server, limited to the chosen scopes, with random ids, an expiry of at most 365 days, and instant revoke that deletes the row and its snapshot. Labs, journal, supplies and weight are off by default. Tokens travel only in the Authorization header, never in the URL, because observability logs every request (head_sampling_rate = 1). The assistant can only propose additions, never edit or delete, and proposals are sealed at rest. The activity log stores tool names and counts, never values. The UI states that tool results go to the AI vendor. Journal notes are returned as clearly marked data to limit prompt injection.

features.name: Clinician visit summary
features.userValue: Appointments are short. A one-page summary (current regimen, adherence, labs against the model, the trend, the patient's questions) helps the clinician decide and helps the patient advocate for themselves. Today's PDF is two raw English-only tables with no chart and no context.
features.ux: Settings > Export > 'Visit summary', and from the Lab page 'Prepare for my appointment'. Options: period (last 3, 6 or 12 months); what to include (current regimen, adherence, lab table, level chart, journal highlights, my questions); language (any of the 7 UI languages, or English for the clinician). The preview looks like the printout. A header with an optional name (off by default) and the date range. 'Current regimen: estradiol valerate 4 mg, injection, every 7 days since 3 Aug'. 'Adherence: 25 of 26 doses on schedule'. A lab table with Date, Measured, Model estimate at that time, and Difference. The estimated-level chart with lab points. 'Personal calibration: reads 12% higher than the population model, fit within ±14%'. A clear note: 'Estimated levels come from a model, not a blood test.' Actions: [Print or save as PDF], [Download PDF], and [Share a link for 7 days], which asks to include labs.
features.technicalFit: src/services/export.ts buildPDFDocument now emits two autoTable tables (Date/Dose/Route/Ester and Date/Test/Level) and is forced to English because jsPDF has no CJK glyphs. Add a print route (a new ViewKey, 'visit-summary') rendered in HTML with an @media print stylesheet, so the browser handles zh, ja, ko, yue and tr fonts and saves to PDF natively, including in the Tauri webview. Keep jsPDF for English downloads and embed the chart by rasterising ResultChart's SVG to canvas and calling doc.addImage. Data sources: calibration.points (CalibrationPoint measured vs model), scale, halfLifeDeltaPct and fitErrPct; schedules and adherence from feature 1; getDoseAdvisory flags; journal highlights from feature 8. For the link, extend SharedDosageSnapshot (sharing.ts) and sanitizeShareSnapshot to version 2 with opt-in labs[], and give PublicShare.tsx a clinician layout.
features.privacy: Generated on the device. Name and username are left out by default. The link option is the existing expiring share, with an optional password, and includes labs only if ticked.

features.name: Injection and patch site rotation
features.userValue: Rotating injection sites cuts down on soreness, lumps and scar tissue, and rotating patch sites reduces skin irritation. People forget which side they used last.
features.ux: Dose form, injection: a 'Site' row with a small body outline and tappable zones (left or right thigh, glute or ventrogluteal, deltoid, and abdomen for subcutaneous). The suggested site is preselected with the text 'Suggested: right thigh, last used 21 days ago', and one tap changes it. Patch: lower abdomen left or right, buttock left or right, upper arm, with 'Avoid left abdomen, used 3 days ago'. History: each entry shows its site ('Right thigh'). A 'Sites' view shows the body map with each zone labelled by days since last use. Optional check-in the next day: 'How is the site?' with Fine, Sore, Lump or Redness. Zones with recent reactions drop to the bottom of the suggestions.
features.technicalFit: DoseEvent.extras holds numbers only, and gel already stores a categorical site as an index (ExtraKey.gelSite + GEL_SITE_ORDER in logic.ts; GelFields.tsx). Add ExtraKey.injectionSite and ExtraKey.patchSite as indexes into new INJECTION_SITE_ORDER and PATCH_SITE_ORDER lists. Extras survive sanitizeImportedEvents (kept wholesale) and are in syncMerge CONTENT_FIELDS.events, so edits sync. Nothing in the PK code iterates extras, so the model is unaffected. Required: buildSharedDosageSnapshot (shareSnapshot.ts) must strip the new keys, or the worker's SHARE_EXTRA_KEYS allowlist makes PUT /api/shares/live fail with INVALID_SNAPSHOT and live links quietly stop updating. The suggestion is the least recently used allowed zone for the route, skipping zones with a recent reaction. Add a picker component to dose_form/InjectionFields.tsx and PatchFields.tsx.
features.privacy: Stays in local data and the E2E backup. Removed from share snapshots, and left out of remote MCP by default.

features.name: Mood, symptom and body journal on the curve
features.userValue: Many people want to know whether low mood, fatigue, hot flashes or breast tenderness line up with their low points (common with long injection intervals), and to track body changes over months. It also gives the clinician concrete observations.
features.ux: Home: a 'How are you today?' row under the chart with a one-tap, labelled 5-step mood scale (icons, not emoji). 'More' opens energy, sleep, libido, symptom chips (hot flashes, headache, breast tenderness, acne, dysphoria, fatigue, other) and a short note of up to 500 characters. Chart: entries appear as small square markers under the time axis. Tapping one shows the entry with context: 'Low energy. Estimated E2 then: about 95 pg/mL, near your low point.' Insights (opt-in, after 20 or more entries): a simple two-column comparison, near the low point versus the rest of the cycle: 'Low mood logged on 6 of 10 days near your low point, and 4 of 30 other days', captioned 'Patterns, not proof'. Body section: optional weight, waist and chest measurements as trend lines. A new weight entry offers 'Use this weight for the model'. Highlights can go into the visit summary.
features.technicalFit: A new synced RecordKind 'journal' in syncMerge.ts: CONTENT_FIELDS [timeH, mood, energy, sleep, symptoms, note, measures], plus tombstones, sanitizer, buildExportPayload and MODE_SUFFIXES (or a shared key, since mood is not tied to a mode). The level at each entry comes from interpolateConcentration_E2(sim, t) × calibrationFn(t), or interpolateConcentration_T. Cycle phase comes from schedule slots (feature 1). ResultChart.tsx gets a `journal` markers prop, rendered like labResults. Size: the whole payload must fit in MAX_CLOUD_BACKUP_BYTES (2 MiB), and 3 entries a day with full notes is about 0.5 MB a year. So cap notes, store symptoms as short codes, and show usage on the Account page. No photos in the backup. Weight entries update the existing synced weight scalar (weight and weight-at, newest wins), because runSimulation takes a single bodyWeightKG today.
features.privacy: The most sensitive data in the app. It lives only on the device and in the E2E backup. It never goes into share snapshots or push payloads. The MCP scope is off by default with an explicit 'includes your notes' warning, and notes are returned as marked, untrusted data.

concepts.name: Tideline
concepts.thesis: The whole app is a single line of time that you scroll through: past above, now at a fixed reading line, future below. Logging something, planning it and being reminded about it all mean putting an item on that line, and the estimated level at any moment is simply whatever sits under the reading line.
concepts.bigIdea:
Scroll to scrub. On a phone the chart is turned 90 degrees and becomes the page. Time runs down the screen: the past is above, and the future continues below, the way a calendar reads. The estimated level is drawn as a narrow vertical lane beside the time labels, with the target range as a flat green stripe through it. Every dose, blood test, reminder, patch, journal note, refill date and assistant suggestion is a row attached to the line at its own time.

The screen has a fixed horizontal "reading line" about 40% of the way down. The big number in the pinned header always shows the level at whatever moment is under that line. When the app opens, that moment is now: "186 pg/mL, in your target range". Scroll up and the header shows the past ("Tue 22 Sep, 21:40, about 196"). Scroll down and it switches to forecast wording ("Sun 27 Sep, 18:00, forecast about 296 if you keep Saturday's dose"). This also fixes the current chart's biggest touch failure, which is that there is no readout: scrolling is the readout, so no hover and no precise tap is needed.

The past and future are separated by tone, not by a gradient. Everything above now sits on a slightly deeper warm paper (#F3EEE6). Everything below sits on plain paper (#FBF8F3). The past curve is a solid terracotta line. The future curve is a dashed blue line inside a flat blue "likely range" band that widens with distance from now, which is an honest way to show uncertainty.

Logging, planning and reminding are one gesture on one line. Tap the Log button, or long-press anywhere on the line, and the dose sheet opens pre-set to that moment. A ghost marker appears on the visible line above the sheet and can be dragged. While the marker is above now, the button reads "Log dose". Once you drag it below the now line, the verb changes to "Plan dose", and a "Repeat" row and a "Remind me" row appear. A repeating plan becomes a schedule, the schedule creates reminders, and the reminders show up ahead of you on the line as blue rows with Log it, Snooze and Skip. Because the line always shows what a dose will do, the ghost preview makes the result concrete before you save: "This dose peaks around 305 pg/mL on Mon evening."

The rest of the app is the same line seen at different zoom levels or through filters:
- History is the line at month zoom, with adherence written as words.
- Blood tests are the black diamonds on the line, plus a strip comparing measured values with the model.
- Plans lists what lies ahead on the line.
- The AI assistant can only put proposals on the line, and nothing is saved until you accept.

On desktop (1440px) the line turns back to horizontal, because time follows the long side of the screen, and the same lanes run under it. People with long injection intervals, patch changes and lab timing questions think in "where am I in my cycle, and what comes next". This layout answers that with no explanation needed.

concepts.name: The daily letter
concepts.thesis: Every screen opens with a few well-set sentences about your body, built from your own data. Every number, date and name in them can be tapped to show where it came from. You answer in the same kind of sentence, and that same sentence grammar is what your AI assistant reads and writes.
concepts.bigIdea:
The app talks first, in plain words. Home is not a dashboard. It is a short letter the app writes fresh each time it opens, and it always keeps the same order so people can learn to scan it: (1) where your level probably is and where it is heading, (2) what is coming up next and how reliably you have kept to it, (3) at most one "worth knowing" item, picked by priority (a dose advisory, then supplies, then a lab-timing suggestion), and (4) an optional postscript for things waiting on your decision, such as an assistant's suggested entry. Every value in the letter is a "live word": a real button, set in the accent ink with a solid tinted underline. Tapping one opens a margin note that says where the number came from ("The standard model gives 160 pg/mL for your doses and weight. Your 4 blood tests say you run 16% higher, so it becomes 186."), the part of the chart behind it, and a way to change it when that makes sense (the target range, the reminder time).

Logging works the same way in reverse. A composer sits at the bottom of Today, Diary and Tests. You type or dictate "4mg ev inj just now" and the app writes back the sentence it understood: "4 mg of estradiol valerate, by injection into your right thigh, today at 14:07." Every slot in that sentence can be tapped to change it with chips. A slot the app could not resolve shows in amber and blocks saving. The app never guesses an amount, and there is always a "Use the form instead" path.

This is out of the box because one pure narration module (sentence templates in 7 languages, with typed slots) drives four surfaces: the Today letter, the share page summary, the printable visit letter for a clinician, and the MCP tool results. When Claude answers "what's my E2 right now?" it reads the same careful sentence the person sees, hedges included ("estimated, not measured, as of 14:05"). When Claude proposes an entry, it arrives as a postscript in the letter that the person accepts or declines. For people on HRT, the questions they open the app with are "am I okay right now?", "when is my next dose?" and "is anything off?". The letter answers those three in about 60 words, readable at a glance, copyable into a message to a clinician, and never hiding that the number is a model estimate.

concepts.name: Rhythm dial
concepts.thesis: Oyama Tracker opens on a single dial that shows where you are in your dosing cycle today, with the next dose as one large button, so looking after the routine takes a glance and one tap, and the curve, the history and the lab maths sit one layer down.
concepts.bigIdea: Most people open an HRT tracker to answer three quick questions: what's next, have I taken it, and am I okay. They don't open it to read a pharmacokinetic chart. The Rhythm dial answers those questions from the shape of the person's own regimen. The dial draws one full cycle as a ring: 7 segments for a weekly EV 4 mg injection, 3.5-day halves for a twice-weekly patch, or a 24-hour clock face with dose slots at 08:00 and 20:00 for sublingual E2 plus CPA. A notch on the outside marks "you are here". Inside the ring, the estimated level for this cycle is wrapped around as a radial trace, and a flat translucent annulus marks the usual range. The peak after the shot and the fall toward the next one become a shape you learn to recognise, without axes or units. In the centre is a large "Day 5 of 7" with a pixel cat whose pose follows the rhythm instead of only the clock. When a dose is due the cat waits by its bowl. Right after a dose is logged it eats and then plays. Mid-cycle it grooms or lies as a loaf. It sleeps at night whatever the schedule says. It never looks sad and it never scolds. Under the dial is the single largest control in the app, and its label depends on the state: "Log estradiol valerate 4 mg" when a dose is due, "Log a dose" otherwise, and "Put on a new patch" on change day. Below that are the three things a routine depends on: Coming up (reminders), Supplies (how long the vial lasts), and a pending assistant suggestion if there is one. Being forgiving is part of the design. A missed slot is drawn as an open outline, never red. The copy reads "Missed Saturday? Log it for when you actually took it, or skip it. Your curve adjusts either way." Adherence appears as a neutral count ("On schedule for 12 of 13 weeks") one layer down, never as a streak. This fits HRT specifically because regimens are cyclical and adherence depends on the rhythm: a weekly or 5-day injector, and someone changing patches every 3.5 days, lose track because the interval is longer than a week or doesn't line up with it. A ring that makes the interval visible, together with one-tap logging from the reminder, also keeps the model accurate, since the curve is only as good as the log.
